name: AI Safety and Alignment
guide:
Day to day, AI safety and alignment work centers on making a model behave the way its builders intend, not just making it more capable. In our data that shows up as postings like OpenAI's Software Engineer, AI Safety and its Technical Program Manager, AI Safety and Safeguards, NVIDIA's Senior Machine Learning Engineer, AI Safety, and ElevenLabs' Data Scientist, AI Safety. Kraken's Senior Software Engineer, Agent Safety and Evals sits in the same territory, evaluating whether an autonomous agent stays within the bounds it was given. The daily work behind these titles is model evaluation, red teaming a system before it ships, writing or enforcing safety policy inside a lab, and interpreting why a model produced a given output.

Readers often lump this in with AI Research or AI Security, but the postings we track separate them clearly. AI Research pushes model capability forward, bigger context windows, new architectures, better benchmarks, regardless of downstream behavior. AI Security protects the company's own infrastructure, data, and pipelines from attackers, closer to traditional cybersecurity work applied to ML systems. AI Safety and Alignment sits in between, asking whether the model itself does what it is supposed to do and refuses what it should not, which is why titles here pair safety with evals, safeguards, or trust and safety rather than with infrastructure or platform.

A PhD or a strong research background matters for roles that sit closer to research, such as NVIDIA's machine learning engineer post or the data scientist and evals roles at Perplexity, ElevenLabs, and Databricks. Companies hiring for those seats are testing candidates on their ability to design evaluation methodology and reason about model behavior, which is graduate level training territory. Roles framed as program management or software engineering, like OpenAI's Technical Program Manager, AI Safety and Safeguards or Kraken's agent safety engineer, lean more on shipping experience than credentials. Certifications are essentially nonexistent in this field. None of the postings we pulled reference any safety or alignment certification, and no such credential shows up anywhere in the skills data attached to these jobs.

The postings skew senior. Of the fifteen roles we tracked, four carry a Senior title, three are Staff level, three are Manager level, one is Lead, and four are Mid level, with none at an entry level. What gets someone hired into this discipline is a track record, either published or demonstrable, in model evaluation or red teaming work that actually shipped, not a general machine learning background. Companies are not hiring people to learn alignment on the job. They want candidates who can point to evaluation frameworks they built or safety issues they caught before a model went out the door.

Python, Rust, and SQL appear across nearly every posting we tracked, alongside recurring mentions of large language models and model evaluation as named skills. NIST shows up repeatedly, at OpenAI, Kraken, and Cortea AI, pointing to the NIST AI risk management framework as a real reference point for safety work rather than an abstract concern. Kraken's listing is the most explicit about method, naming red teaming and threat modeling directly alongside LangChain. Cloud and infrastructure tools, AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, and Terraform, turn up often enough to show that many of these roles are embedded ML engineering positions with a safety mandate, not standalone research seats.

We currently track approximately 8 open postings in AI Safety and Alignment as of today, out of 15 total postings in our database for this category. Salary figures are rare here. Only 2 of those 15 postings carry salary data, both from NVIDIA for the same Senior Machine Learning Engineer, AI Safety title, ranging from $249,561 to $262,704 per year depending on location. The companies that show up most often hiring in this category are OpenAI, NVIDIA, ElevenLabs, and Cortea AI, each appearing more than once in our data. This is a small, specialized slice of the AI job market, and the postings reflect that, senior leaning, evaluation heavy, and concentrated at a handful of labs and infrastructure companies rather than spread broadly.

reading.body:
Eight active job openings for AI safety and alignment roles across leading AI labs and infrastructure companies suggest the field is moving from research to operations. Every posting emphasizes evaluation, measurement, and systematic quality control, not theoretical work.

The concentration of these roles at OpenAI, Perplexity, Deepgram, and Databricks reflects a shift in where safety work happens: embedded in product teams building and deploying models rather than isolated in research groups. Evals and trust infrastructure are now operational necessities, not afterthoughts. This mirrors the broader pattern where capability at scale requires systematic measurement to remain controllable.

The data does not reveal hiring volume trends, budget allocation to safety relative to other functions, or whether these openings represent growth or replacement. It captures a snapshot of posted positions, not filled roles or internal team sizes. It shows geography and remote flexibility but does not indicate whether safety talent is concentrating or dispersing across geographies.
